en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Having paid homage to the most excellent Jewel and relying upon the venerable ones of old, [I shall explain] the Dhamma-method.
I shall proclaim the Nitidhamma, which brings happiness to the entire world:
the teacher and the craft, wisdom and learning, wealth and speech,
the country and the support, the friend, the wicked person, the virtuous person, and strength.
The woman, the son, and the slave; the householder, the ascetic, and the one who has gone forth;
the one to be known, the ornament, and the one who serves the duties of a king;
the mixed pairs and so forth, and the miscellaneous—this is the summary outline.
Those whose feet are fragrant with perfumes, yet who have no fine garments here,
and who are covered only by the dust of their own feet— they alone are the virtuous ones who dwell in solitude.
A fool desires to adorn himself even without the scent of perfume or the edge of a garment.
How indeed could a wise person fail to attain the state of laughter?
A wise person should please their teacher by rising for them, attending upon them,
being obedient, serving them, and by learning the craft with diligence.
He who serves with diligence his preceptors and teachers, as well as his mother and father—
even though he has heard much, he is like one who has heard nothing at all.
He who serves with diligence his preceptors and teachers, as well as his mother and father...
He attends with care, and his learning is likewise;
having investigated thoroughly both the syllables and the instructions.
One who destroys his enemies, one who is heavy with the burden of wealth, a maker of thieves,
one endowed with wisdom and learning— wherever such a person exists, he is called "wealthy."
One who desires to know that state must go to a great master.
Just as the shade of a tree is pleasant, so too is the lineage of one's father and mother;
after that, the teacher; after that, the king; and after that, the teaching of the Victor.
The stone parasol and the heavy burden, then the gods and the Nacikkha fire;
then the instruction for the elders, and then the teaching of the Conqueror.
The balance and the lightness in the world, and then the one of fickle nature.
The address of elders, the non-neglect of the ascetic’s duty,
learning, conventional designations, numbers, the yogas, and likewise the distinctions;
musicians, courtesans, archery, the Vedas, and the Pūraṇas.
Medicine, history, light, magic, poetry, flags, and sounds—these are the eighteen arts.
From laziness comes no craft; from no craft comes no wealth.
For one who does not give, whence can there be a friend? For one who is not a friend, whence can there be happiness?
For one who is not happy, whence can there be merit? For one who lacks merit, whence can there be Nibbāna?
There is no wealth equal to a craft; thieves do not seize a craft.
The craft of this world is friendship, which brings happiness in the world beyond.
The Buddha is the eternal sun for his sons; do not weary the Teacher, who is your preceptor.
A king is honored in his own country, but the Buddha is honored everywhere.
The son of awakening is one who is free from laziness, while the non-awakened is a bearer of burdens.
In this world, the awakened are honored day after day, more so than the sons of awakening.
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of noble lineages—
Those devoid of learning do not shine, like scentless *kiṃsuka* trees.
One who has a mother as an enemy and was not trained during childhood does not shine in the midst of an assembly, just as a crow does not shine among swans.
One who has reached the highest state of virtue does not dwell on a high bed;
his dwelling is at the pinnacle of a palace. What would a crow do as a garuḍa?
He masters all that is heard—whether inferior, superior, or middling.
One should know the purpose of everything, but one should not employ everything.
The deluded person in this world does not shine,
even if they praise only their own self.
Even when the well is covered over,
it is illuminated by the light of knowledge;
therefore, do not indulge in pride toward the wicked for the sake of subduing the intoxicated.
The fire that produces the activity of the eye is like darkness to owls;
eating, sexual intercourse,
and sleep exist even in a cowherd.
Through a particular branch of knowledge,
a man may become equal to a cowherd;
yet through greed for his craft, that same man may acquire great wealth.
One who sees a dream at dawn is unable to describe it to another.
Hearing increases through attentive listening, and learning increases wisdom.
Through wisdom one understands the meaning; when the meaning is understood, it brings happiness.
Seeing a danger yet to come, one should avoid it from afar;
seeing a danger already arrived, the wise person stands firm against it.
Greed, anger, intoxication, pride, sloth, envy, and negligence—these one should abandon.
The wise man should abandon gluttony, sloth, and hypocrisy, as well as stinginess.
One who is endowed with these seven qualities— faith, moral shame,
moral dread, great learning, energy, and wisdom— is considered a true sage.
Whatever benefit there is in this present life,
and whatever benefit pertains to the future world— the steadfast one, through the realization of these benefits, [attains them].
He is truly called a wise man.
He who understands speech that accords with one's true nature, affection that accords with one's true nature,
and anger that accords with one's true nature— he is a wise man.
A king is never equal to a wise man at any time;
though a king is honored in his own country, the Buddha is honored everywhere.
For the sake of praising the wise man, punishment is inflicted upon the fool.
Just as one who is truly wise would praise what is truly praised,
so too, by means of his own single self, a wise man should subdue the great masses of people who are led astray; he should destroy anger within himself.
There is an exceedingly vast difference between the physical body and its virtues:
the body perishes in an instant, while virtues endure for an aeon.
Having attained great wealth, as well as knowledge and excellence, [one should practice virtue].
One who reflects without being stubborn is called wise.
They do not crave what cannot be obtained, nor do they grieve for what is lost;
they do not become bewildered by adversity—that is why they are truly wise.
A wise person should not despise even a single word at the point of a knot;
for what can a mere heap of reeds do against one who brings light to the three great islands?
One who seeks their own welfare should avoid both virtues and faults with equal indifference.
To the delicate lotus, the reed becomes harsh.
Those who are highly learned and bear great weapons fall into ruin when they harbor doubts regarding the cutting away of the iron-like [defilements], being deluded by greed.
Having seen both faults and virtues, one who speaks of virtues is like a tamer of elephants;
for the world does not perceive a speck of collyrium even when it is present.
A wise person of steady mind would never, even once, enter into association with such a one.
May I attain my own welfare, the welfare of others, and the bliss that culminates in Nibbāna.
Just as there is no well on a riverbank, nor fire-drills, palm-fronds, or salt;
and just as there is no new water-pipe or such things—so too are words that do not issue from the mouth.
The wise man remains silent when unasked, but speaks when questioned, like a rain-cloud;
the fool, however, whether asked or unasked, always boasts excessively.
He who is adorned with the perfection of virtues brings benefit to all living beings.
One should not practice for the sake of another alone; how could such a person be wise?
A hero should practice for the sake of both himself and others; if he is unable to do so for both, he should at least practice for his own sake;
and if even that is impossible, he should at least free himself from evil.
One who hears everything with the ear of wisdom and sees everything with the eye of wisdom—
the wise one does not grieve over what has been seen or heard, for he is worthy of knowing all.
Just as a blind man might possess sight, or a deaf man might possess hearing;
Like a wise man who is mute at a water-tank,
or like a strong man who is weak when it comes to wealth— if, when these matters arise,
one were to lie down as if dead, the wise desire a son who is superior or equal to themselves.
They do not desire one who is base-born and from a family of broken lineage.
Among these three wise men in the world, I am indeed the superior speaker;
I too am a speaker, yet they do not wish for me.
One who is peaceful through the attainment of peace in the assembly,
who does not dance nor speak according to the Dhamma,
having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion—
The virtuous, while speaking the Dhamma,
do not commit an offense even toward fools, the intoxicated, kings, teachers,
mothers, fathers, the Saṅgha, or elder brothers. The wise do not commit a fault in such cases.
A wise person should avoid self-praise and self-blame, as well as misconduct at home,
deception, and contempt. One should also avoid another's wife,
intoxicants, and throwing clods of earth at others' property.
The wise person who observes all beings as his own self— avoiding deceitful friendship,
impure conduct, and the pursuit of success through the harming of others— [attains prosperity].
One who desires the welfare of others should,
like a wise man, skillfully and subtly investigate a woman with pleasant speech and harshness, having discerned her well.
Just as food cooked on a seven-spoked spit remains in the vessel,
so too do those standing far away take wealth from a mountain rich in gems;
likewise, fools remain near the wise.
As gold [is distinguished] from deer, as one of good conduct from the immoral,
and as the righteous from the unrighteous, what is the use of learning even for a fool?
This man of little learning lives like a tethered ox.
One who is ignorant grows in flesh and sinews, while one who possesses wisdom does not grow [in such things].
The conceited person, having heard little, considers what he has heard to be much;
like a frog in a well who has never seen the waters of the Indus, he remains narrow-minded.
Therefore, know this as well: in the puddles and at their banks, the small puddles resound, but the great ocean remains silent.
The virtuous say that what is well-spoken is supreme.
Speaking dharma instead of non-dharma is the second;
speaking what is pleasant instead of what is unpleasant is the third;
and speaking truth instead of falsehood is the fourth.
Just as gold from the Siṃhamedā river does not remain when placed among base metals,
so the speech and discourse of the wise do not remain among the wicked.
This splendor is indeed great splendor, for it is not soft toward the clay-like and the cruel.
One who is gentle wins over even those who are harsh;
with gentleness one conquers the cruel; there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through gentleness, for it is by means of gentleness that one achieves victory.
Sandalwood is cool in the world, and even the moon is cooler than that;
yet, O Sandalwood and Moon, well-spoken words are cooler still.
One whose speech is cool gains many friends, while one who is harsh gains only enemies.
In this regard, a comparison should be understood by means of the moon, the sun, and the king:
even a small word spoken at the proper time and on a suitable occasion becomes well-spoken;
even a single mouthful of coarse food, when eaten, can become delicious.
Those who speak much like a weapon and those who talk excessively without respect—
have you not seen the river water that, though beneficial, remains indifferent?
One should not speak beyond measure, nor should one always be silent.
One should utter speech that is coherent and measured at the appropriate time.
In all desired undertakings, skill in speech is the root;
for one who lacks skill in speech, the desired goal is not accomplished.
Hands, feet, blood, back, belly, and face— these are what people always resort to when they are well-instructed. Faith is wealth,
virtue is wealth, and the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame is wealth.
The wealth of the learned is generosity, and wisdom is the seventh kind of wealth.
For women, beauty is wealth; for men, noble lineage is wealth;
for serpents, venom is wealth; and for kings, military power is wealth.
Virtue is the wealth of bhikkhus, and knowledge is the wealth of brahmins.
Neither physical beauty nor wisdom, neither noble birth nor lineage—
when time is either unfavorable or favorable— it is wealth alone that makes the difference.
Even sons, wives, and brothers abandon one who is destitute of wealth;
they wait upon the wealthy man. In this world, wealth is a great friend.
Beings serve those who possess it, whether it be water, food, or anything else.
Both enjoyment and wealth must be abandoned; for these are empty things.
Misfortune is brought about by oneself, and misfortune is produced by oneself;
for neither fortune nor misfortune is caused by one person for another.
King Dhanavāja and Utiyo, as well as these Nadī and Vejjā—
these five places do not exist today, nor did they dwell there on that day.
In whatever land one has no equal, no joy, and no kinsmen.
One should not dwell for even a single day with anyone who has no knowledge of the Vedas,
nor with one who does not honor the truth. One should not dwell for even a single day with those who seek to cause dishonor,
nor with those who show contempt for the virtuous, nor even with those who honor the base.
The lion, the good man, and the elephant go astray from their paths;
yet they meet their end right there, while the crow, the base man, and the deer perish elsewhere.
Where the lazy man is honored as if he were wise, and the hero is treated with contempt like a coward;
Those who do not dwell on what is non-existent dwell in peace, being free from the sense of distinction.
The wise man moves with one foot and stands firm with the other;
he does not look at the ground ahead, nor does he abandon the path already traversed.
The teeth, hair, nails, and skin are beautiful when they remain in their proper places;
thus one should understand the mind, and abandon both crookedness and haste.
Even one who possesses virtues equal to those of the Omniscient One will sink if he lacks support.
A priceless jewel, a gem, shines when set in gold.
One should not serve a harsh master, nor should one serve a miserly master;
rather, one should serve a master who does not oppress, and never one who over-exacts.
One should not associate with such a person who destroys one's virtues behind one's back and speaks falsely even to one's face—
like one tempted by a pot of poison. One may associate with those who are gentle behind one's back,
and one may associate with those who are like the interior of a fire.
Bowing with his whole body to his master, he was not deluded regarding the world beyond.
He did not associate with those who commit evil deeds alone, nor with those who speak falsely;
he did not associate with those intent on their own self-interest, nor with those who are excessively haughty.
Having relied upon a great support, even a small being may attain a great existence;
by relying on a mountain of gold, one becomes a golden-winged bird.
Even if one is without companions or lacking in strength, what can a person of fiery energy not accomplish?
A fire established in a place sheltered from the wind extinguishes by itself.
Depending on a tree and a beautiful plot of ground, flowers and fruits flourish;
depending on a true person, great merit flourishes.
One who is not envious, not harsh, not deceitful, pure, and truthful in speech;
one who is not greedy and desires the welfare of others—that person is called the supreme man.
One who restrains others from what is harmful and enjoins them toward what is beneficial;
Not abandoning one in misfortune is, in brief, the characteristic of a friend.
In times of illness, in times of misfortune, during famine, in times of conflict,
at the king’s gate, and at the cemetery— this is the brief definition of a friend.
A virtuous person is like a physician who possesses both skill and medicine, who is wise,
provides rare nourishment, and is as sweet and disease-removing as excellent medicine.
He who abandons what is permanent and devotes himself to what is impermanent— [is truly wise].
The talk of those who are unstable will not reach those who are stable.
One should seize the greedy with wealth, the stubborn with forceful action,
the deluded by complying with their desires, and the wise as they truly are.
Through constant association, by not meeting together,
and by requesting at the improper time— by these means friends decay.
Therefore, one should not go too often, nor should one go after long intervals.
One should ask a favor at the proper time; in this way, friends do not perish.
If through association with a certain friend one’s security in yoga is lost, a wise person should avoid that person beforehand, just as one guards against fire.
Through association with a friend by whom security from bondage increases,
the wise person should act toward him as an equal in all matters. Like the bamboo,
which grows higher and higher, reaching for the essence of the sweet fruit.
Thus the Sage spoke concerning those few worldly phenomena,
as well as those supramundane phenomena that lead to Nibbāna— phenomena that are wholesome,
virtuous, and conducive to liberation, while others are the opposite, unwholesome, and leading to suffering.
By relying on a virtuous friend, all these qualities come to living beings;
therefore, one should indeed show great respect toward virtuous friends.
He who is wise, knowing and having realized for himself...
One who possesses firm devotion to a virtuous friend performs his duties with care for one who is suffering;
such a person is called a "true man" in the world.
A kinsman is one intent on your welfare, while a friend is one intent on your benefit;
illness is harmful to the body, whereas forest medicine is beneficial.
His face is like a lotus, and his speech is cool as sandalwood.
On the tip of the tongue there is honey, but in the heart is the deadly poison;
one should not associate with such a person, but should avoid that friend.
Having performed unwholesome deeds, and having performed wholesome deeds in the past...
Whether one is happy or suffering, the fool does not see the lower realms (apāya).
Through procrastination, he neglects the practice of giving, virtue, and so forth;
though unstable, he imagines himself to be stable and eternal.
Having committed a foolish and evil deed, one does not dare to stand before it;
for what lion, as he goes along, would dare to soil his own footprints?
Even a poor man desires wealth, and a weakling longs for power.
One who is slow-witted, one who engages in disputes, and one with a threefold mark of delusion;
one who acts without being summoned, one who speaks much without being asked,
and one who praises his own virtues— this is the threefold mark of inferiority.
Just as a raw mango ripens from the outside while the inside remains unripe,
and the interior is filled with maggots— such is the nature of the wicked.
That which is deficient is considered rotten, while that which is full is indeed peaceful.
The fool is like a half-filled jar, while the wise man is like a full jar.
Even when treated with respect by the wise, a wicked person displays many pretenses;
like a glowing ember being crushed, he only emits black smoke.
Through instruction given to a foolish pupil, through supporting a young wife,
and through association with wicked enemies, even a wise man comes to ruin.
Through beauty for the sake of another's wife, and through wealth for the sake of worldly fame;
With their shoulders drooping and their noses turned downward, possessing qualities even more base than the base themselves—
there is nothing in this world more ridiculous than these people.
The wicked man says, "This person is wicked," while he himself is truly a wicked person.
Indeed, the wicked and the base take delight in slandering others;
having become the essence of all flavors, they are not satisfied with purity.
Through excessive intimacy, one is satiated; through servility, one becomes weak.
How can the mind of a wicked person be compared to iron? Therefore,
one who desires their own welfare and possesses discernment should avoid the company of the wicked from afar, as if avoiding a venomous serpent.
Association with the wicked is not conducive to one’s welfare,
just as a glowing ember, though still hot, causes peace and blackness [of the skin];
even if adorned with knowledge, the wicked person is to be avoided.
Though adorned with jewels and being virtuous, performing every kind of service for both [sides], he was consumed by fire; even the wind, his friend, became his enemy.
Thus, through wickedness, even friendship can destroy one's refuge.
One who is wicked toward everyone is more wicked than anyone else;
he must be subdued by means of spells and medicines, yet he is not pacified by a mere threshing-floor.
Even one who is virtuous in heart and learned cannot subdue a wicked person.
Through association with the honey, even the hollow of a tree becomes sweet;
through association with the unvirtuous, even a virtuous person becomes unvirtuous.
Just as a path covered in refuse becomes foul, even a lotus becomes unpleasant.
Just as a fisherman draws in a putrid fish with the tip of a hook,
or as reeds are carried away by a stench, so too is the consequence of associating with fools.
One should not look upon a fool, nor hear him, nor dwell together with a fool.
One should not engage in conversation or discourse with a fool, nor should one find pleasure in doing so.
The witless person leads others to ruin and yokes them to burdens they cannot bear;
he is difficult to lead aright, and even when treated properly, he becomes angry.
One who does not know the discipline has no vision of what is truly good.
Even if a fool attends upon a wise person for as long as his life lasts,
he does not understand the Dhamma, just as one cannot perceive the flavor of the broth in a bamboo tube.
The fruit strikes down the plantain tree, and the bamboo strikes down the fruit;
honor strikes down a base man, just as a foal struck down its mother.
A dog, seeing another dog, shows its teeth in order to bark.
Seeing an evil person as an evil person, one who is angry seeks to harm them.
Is not even a frog like a lion? Is not even a pig like a leopard?
Is not even a tiger like a rat? And is not even one of poor wisdom like a wise man?
Like a frog and a lion,
like a crow and a crane,
and like a child and a wise man.
The elephant is corrupted by its tail;
the crow and the owl are corrupted by their nests; the rat is corrupted by its home;
the monkey is corrupted by the forest; and among humans, the brahmin is corrupted.
Grass, firewood, earth, and water—the fourth being well-spoken words—these four things are found in every household and are never exhausted. People drink the water, but not the lord;
people eat the fruit of the trees, but not the lord.
The wealth of those intent on the welfare of others is like a rain-cloud that never fails to give water;
though dwelling far away, they perform the service of a messenger through their virtues.
Just as bees go toward a ketaka flower after smelling its fragrance, so do they seek out the virtuous.
One should not walk with those who are crowded with wicked companions,
nor with those who are unrefined, nor with many born of low birth,
nor with the intoxicated. Having avoided evil friends, one should associate with the supreme person.
One who aspires to unshakable happiness should abide by his teacher’s instruction.
Just as a jackfruit, though green on the outside and with its stalk still attached,
is full of nectar within— such is the nature of the virtuous.
Just as one who wraps himself in the leaves of the tagara-plant is perfumed by their fragrance,
so too does association with the wise perfume the mind.
See the wise, listen to the wise, and dwell together with the wise.
One should engage in conversation and discourse with the wise and find delight in doing so.
The intelligent person leads others by right method and does not yoke them to what is improper;
through right guidance he becomes excellent, and being well-spoken of, he is not disturbed.
One understands the discipline through association with the virtuous.
Even by a small amount, a wise person who attends upon a sage quickly understands the Dhamma,
just as the tongue perceives the flavor of soup.
Physical strength, the power of ministers, the power of wealth, and the power of noble birth—among these four powers, the power of wisdom is the most excellent.
For birds, the sky is their strength; for fish, water is their strength.
The king’s strength is his army; the princes’ strength is their retinue.
The moon’s strength is its light; the hero’s strength is his valor. The strength of recluses and brahmins is their self-control;
the ocean’s strength is its shore. And the supreme strength of a woman is her husband.
The lion has strength with its forefeet; the spotted deer has greater strength than that;
the kippilika bird has more strength than that; but the king is the strongest of all.
The forest is the domain of wild beasts; the sky is the domain of winged birds.
The destination of those whose nature has reached dispassion is the state of Nibbāna, the goal of the Arahants.
A wise man born of noble family should conduct himself with composure, whether he is with one who is unattractive or one who is beautiful,
regarding even a lowly marriage as equal to a wedding of the most handsome.
One with eyes like those of a deer, beautiful hair, a slender waist, and even teeth;
one with a lovely complexion and a deep navel;
and one who is virtuous and diligent in mind—even such a person may carry away a man from a lowly family.
She fed her mother-in-law, supported her daughters-in-law, and was devoted to her own kin in their duties;
she honored those who had performed good deeds.
She was always established in the Dhamma and was beautiful in her conduct even upon her bed.
A woman who is highly esteemed as the best among women,
who always supports her father-in-law and mother-in-law with diligence,
and who does not despise her husband— the provider who brings all her desires— is truly noble.
Nor should she cause her husband to act according to his whims;
the wise honor all those who are venerable to their husband.
Diligent and untiring, she should be one who unites the members of the household.
She enjoys what is pleasing to her husband and protects his accumulated wealth.
Thus does a noble woman conduct herself, following the will and desires of her husband;
she is reborn among those gods who delight in what is pleasing, wherever she may arise.
The Sage has declared that even a single woman may be called a "bedfellow";
indeed, a woman is the best of all possessions and the foremost of attendants.
Yet, one who lacks discernment [does not see her as such] whether she be mother, daughter, or sister.
O sage, do not dwell in seclusion, for women are full of guile.
Women imitate the flickering instability of lightning,
the extreme sharpness of weapons, and the ferocity of wind and fire.
Food has two qualities,
wisdom has four qualities,
and effort has six qualities.
In the arising of the eight qualities of passion,
for each and every woman, there were eight husbands: one who was brave,
one who was fickle, and those who brought the essence of all sensual pleasures.
One should not harbor desire for what is new; one who is arrogant is never filled.
One who is quarrelsome is full of envy; those who see [the truth] have overcome craving.
Those who eat to excess sleep like the dead; one should abandon even a son who is a father’s enemy.
One might catch the wind with a net, or hold the ocean in a single hand,
but no man could ever satisfy the minds of women— even as they laugh at one thing,
look with longing at another, and think of yet another.
One should sprinkle one's own kinsmen with the water of silence;
one should not release them through negligence. This is the low nature of women:
that even a man who possesses a thousand tongues might live for a hundred years [yet remain unsatisfied].
He who has spoken with his own handiwork and has reached the destruction of the three stains and doubts— seeing five grounds, the wise desire a son:
"He will support me when I am supported, or he will perform my duties."
May the family lineage endure for a long time, may it receive its inheritance,
or else may it provide offerings to the departed.
The wise desire a son who is either superior or equal to themselves.
They do not desire one who is base-born and of a broken lineage.
Those born from the same womb are not of equal status;
they are of different colors and different behaviors, just like the jujube fruit and its thorns.
Taming is difficult for one with many faults, but taming is easy for one with many virtues;
therefore, O son and disciple, you should tame yourselves at the proper time.
You should exhort and instruct one another.
One should avoid what is unwholesome;
the tamed person becomes beloved,
while the untamed person becomes disliked.
One should admonish even a son or a brother who is wicked, and not abandon them;
for what need is there to cut off hands and feet if one has already been smeared with impurity?
Born within the household, purchased with wealth, he has himself entered into servitude.
From the slave to the king’s counselor, thus there would be four types:
slaves, thieves, friends, and those like kinsmen;
likewise, they are to be understood by the wise as friends, wives, and relatives.
A wife who is ill-disposed, a servant who speaks insolently,
and living with one who is stingy— even in one's own home— there is no doubt that death will come.
People avoid from afar a man who aspires only to gain fame and profit.
Therefore, having disregarded that path, the wise man should seek his own way.
Just as one who goes frequently to a threshing floor, a rice field, a barley field,
or a paddy field would have a measured amount of grain stored away and would cook a measured amount at home.
Having seen the exhaustion of collyrium, the accumulation of anthills, and the gathering of honey, a wise person should dwell at home.
One should know for oneself one's own rise and fall;
one should know for oneself what has been done and what has not been done.
One who should be restrained, he restrains; one who should be encouraged, he encourages.
The noble person is a single-watchman;
the wise person is a two-watchman.
One who possesses the three Amogharāvas,
one who has gone beyond the four Yāmas,
and one who is intent on the welfare of kinsmen—
A son is for the sake of support;
a friend is for the sake of trust;
a wife is for the sake of peace.
One who loves those with faith does not count a hundred coins as much;
one who loves those without faith counts even a single māsaka as a hundred.
Even a beggar is dear, but one who does not grant a request is not dear.
Therefore, O best of men in this world, regarding wealth, craft, and possessions:
one should always protect one's wealth, and one should also protect one's wife and wealth;
one should always remain intent on protecting one's wife, wealth, and oneself.
One should not eat sweet food alone, nor should one eat with a wife who is not common to both;
one should not pursue worldly talk, for that does not increase wisdom.
One who is endowed with the turning of virtue, heedful, and discerning—
Humble in conduct, free from stubbornness, gentle, friendly, and mild;
a gatherer of friends, one who shares and is discerning—
one should always satisfy with food and drink the recluses and brahmins.
One who desires the Dhamma should be a bearer of the heard teachings and one who asks questions;
one should respectfully attend upon those who are virtuous and learned.
The wise person has the head in the east, while long life has the head in the south.
Peace of mind comes from the western direction; death occurs when facing north in the next life.
One’s lifespan is in the east; wealth arises when facing south.
One enjoys fame when facing west; one should not eat while facing north.
One who sits on a thick mat becomes stout; one who stands grows strong;
one who walks about gains long life; and one who runs is free from disease.
Furthermore, he who regards cold and heat as equal to a bed of grass—such a person is called a true recluse.
One should perform the duties of a superior person, dwelling in ease and comfort.
Just as gold is taken from ore, fire from wood, and water from a lowly place,
so too should one acquire knowledge even from a lowly person, for a seeker of jewels does not discriminate based on caste.
A man who awakens another to a secret matter that has not yet been understood will endure being treated as a slave out of fear of the disclosure of his counsel.
Even one who is equal to the fire-god (Jātavedas) [in power] cannot escape when he has lost control over his own ignorance.
The wise person should practice forgiveness, even when provoked by threats of violence.
In matters of wealth, grain, and business, as well as in the pursuit of knowledge and learning,
and in the dispatching of messengers and speech, one should always remain free from shame.
The act of clearing a thorn does not depend upon an agent;
therefore, one should have all tasks performed with something remaining unfinished.
One should extricate an enemy by means of that very enemy who has done one a favor.
One should follow him as a foot-follower follows the heel, like one thorn removing another.
One who shares his own portion with him should share it with others;
one who performs his duties should perform his own duties.
One should not do what is beneficial for one who does not desire one's welfare;
nor should one cultivate intimacy with one who does not cultivate it.
One should avoid the conduct of those whose affection is fickle.
One should not associate with one who has a mind of ill-will;
knowing him to be like a fruitless tree that provides shade,
the world of great serpents would look elsewhere for another.
One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of a family; one should sacrifice a family for the sake of a village;

one should sacrifice a village for the sake of a district; and one should sacrifice even the earth for the sake of oneself. One should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a limb, and even a limb for the sake of the whole person.
One might sacrifice a limb while protecting one's life;
one might even sacrifice wealth, a limb,
and indeed one's entire life, while recollecting the Dhamma.
Coming and going, they take away the life of beings here;
therefore, let them proceed with heedfulness in the teaching of the Conqueror.
For those who come together, peace does not decay for them.
One who endures the excellence of wisdom, one who understands the instruction,
one deluded regarding fire, water, women, snakes, kings, and noble families—
such a person should be understood as one who intentionally approaches those things that snatch away life from mortals.
Even a weapon must be considered as not yet firmly grasped;
even a king who has been won over must be suspected from above;
even a young woman who has come into one's hand must be guarded.
The Teacher is like a well-guided young woman;
diligence is like a friend who brings wealth; laziness is like a friend who brings ruin;
poison is like knowledge that lasts for only a watch of the night; negligence is like nectar turned to poison.
One should abandon even a friend who is a burden for as long as the future lasts,
just as one would break a clay pot with a stone when the time has come.
One should give up a horned beast for fifty hands [in measure], and a vehicle for a hundred.
With a thousand elephants and the sovereignty over the land, one should abandon the wicked person—
whether they be one’s own parents before one’s eyes, or friends and kinsmen out of sight,
or servants and employees in the workplace, or even sons and wives who are held dear.
Skill in arts, wealth acquired through skill, climbing a mountain with skill, one who releases from desire with skill,
and one who releases from anger with skill— these are the five skilled ones.
He who has a hundred eyes and a hundred ears is always the son of the Leader.
Nevertheless, it is the nature of those who lack a leader to be like the blind and the deaf.
It is exceedingly difficult to bring many people of little faith into harmony;
even as a rope is twisted from blades of grass, so too is a king bound by his subjects.
If anger should arise, one should reflect on the simile of the saw;
if craving for flavors should arise, one should reflect on the simile of the son’s flesh.
Generosity is the medicine for affection, and stinginess is the medicine for hatred.
Generosity is the best medicine for misfortune, while stinginess is a drug that causes its own ruin.
One should desire wealth from trade, a craft from those who are highly learned,
a son from a virtuous woman, and a minister from one who has attained his goal.
A person who, having made a large banyan tree or the like—with its small seed yet abundant fruit—their witness, would neglect to perform meritorious or evil deeds;
or one who behaves with lowliness toward those worthy of respect; [such a person is reborn as a tree].
Having destroyed the state of inferiority, one establishes oneself in the highest goal.
One conquers the superior by prostration, the brave by breaking their ranks,
the inferior by a small gift, and the equal by valorous stride.
One should know the fault of being late, and one should know the fault of others [being late];
like a tortoise hiding its limbs, one should observe the conduct of others and perceive their decline.
Sleeping at the wrong time, laziness, irritability, and excessive sleepiness—these are the faults.
Going alone with a single companion, consorting with another’s wife—
these things will lead to the Brahmin’s own harm. Drinking liquor, being intoxicated,
attending festivals, and frequenting the houses of harlots;
Those who are addicted to pleasure, devoid of asceticism, and have evil friends—these people, though possessing great wealth, perish; this is the fruit of a base nature.
Too cold, too hot, and too late—it has become thus.
When the work has been thus entrusted to the young men who have completely squandered their opportunities,
the one who was previously the destroyer is himself destroyed by the destruction of another;
he rushes toward his own ruin like a lion toward its own death, like one who set fire to a grass hut.
One should not place trust in a friend who is untrustworthy, nor should one trust even a friend who is trustworthy.
For a friend who is occasionally provoked to anger reveals all one's faults.
One should avoid a bad country, a bad friend, a bad alliance, and a bad kinsman.
One should avoid from afar King Kuddālaka and King Cakora.
A crab goes about with its head held high, yet it falls into every trap;
likewise, the sons of the hen, the Nīkukkuṭīs, are treated with contempt by men.
A king whose son is base, a wise man whose son is foolish,
and a merchant whose son is poor— these are held in contempt by men.
One should not cause a marriage alliance with someone with whom one does not wish to have a connection.
The connection between the matter and the dispute, the demonstration of the evidence in the absence [of the defendant],
the remainder of the debt, the remainder of the fire, and likewise the remainder of the battle.
They increase again and again;
therefore, one should make an end to them.
A son of noble birth, born of a good family, well-guarded in his lineage;
Even if one has fallen into suffering oneself, one should not perform a base deed.

Just as Samiddha was not satisfied with mere grain and rice, nor Kaṭṭha with grass and fire, so too one who is utterly ruined by misfortune should not commit an evil act. Therefore, one should not do what is wicked.
One should go to the top of a mountain devoid of trees; when the work is accomplished, the fruit is equal.
Through the ripening of karma, one becomes harsh; one should speak with a gentle nature.
Like the smoke of a fool’s anger, it is like water in a swamp where women abound.
Constant consumption of excessive food at night causes the exhaustion of life.
Trust is not appropriate toward women or wicked people;
it is especially so during the summer, by day, in the case of disease, and within the royal court.
Conflict arising from improper work,
battle with the Sangha by those of great power,
and constant treachery toward women— these are always [to be avoided].
The wise man, knowing the doors that lead to death,
should not serve women excessively, nor eat what is unwholesome though it be sweet;
he should honor the elders and not associate with those who are deceitful.
One should not go for the sake of destruction, nor to the battlefield of heroes;
likewise, the wise man, the traveler, and the merchant [should not go] on a journey to a foreign land.
Through the words "Give," the five deities residing in the body [are invoked].
The reproachful cry "Shame on you!", as well as the words "I lack intelligence,
modesty, and glory," the painful words "Give [to me]," and likewise the phrases "There is nothing" and "Give [it]!"—
may these never arise for me in birth after birth.
Where people do not recognize one by birth or by lineage,
there no act of respect is performed toward such a person, even if they are well-known among the folk.
For harsh speech from a mother is inferior, and misconduct from a father is inferior.
One who lacks both mother and father is one of evil speech and evil conduct;
but for one whose mother is excellent, there is good speech, and for one whose father is excellent, there is good conduct.
Both mother and father are supreme;
well-spoken words and good deeds are supreme.
One who is excessively long-lived is greatly deluded; one of medium length is discerning.
Placing Vāsudeva at the forefront, all those of dwarfish appearance proclaim his conduct, proclaim his region,
proclaim his speech, proclaim his origin, and proclaim his food.
The measure of water is the lotus stalk;
the measure of a family is the performance of deeds;
the measure of wisdom is the speech that has been spoken.
They know a good horse by its speed, and a draft animal by its burden;
they know a cow by its milk, and a wise man by his speech.
One should know that food is for the sake of sustenance, a kinsman is for support in times of fear,
a friend is for times of misfortune, and a wife is for times of loss of wealth. Yet,
even all those who possess the light of wisdom do not realize that time exists for the purpose of destruction.
They know [the origins] from the Kukkutāpana [forest], from there the trees, and from there the mountains.
Meru is the ornament of the earth; the moon is the ornament of the night;
the king is the ornament of people; the elephant is the ornament of armies.
Beauty is adorned by virtue,
a family is adorned by conduct,
and another is adorned by flowers.
The strength of the elephant is its splendor;
the beauty of cuckoos is their song; the beauty of women is their husband;
the beauty of the formless is knowledge; and the beauty of ascetics is patience.
Kisā Sobhā and Tapassī,
Thūlā Sobhā and Catuppada,
Vijjā Sobhā and Manussa—
A woman is the beauty of her husband.
Without the night, there is no moon; without waves, there is no ocean;
without swans, there is no blossoming lotus; and without a woman, there is no man.
An ornament for one devoid of clothing; a woman for one devoid of a husband;
a man for one devoid of craft; food for one devoid of a cow.
The moon is the lamp for the world; the husband is the lamp for the wife.
The Dhamma is the lamp of the three worlds; a good son is the lamp of the family.
An empty house is one without a son; a country is empty without a king;
a face is empty without wisdom; everything is empty for the poor.
With earrings made of the gold he had heard from others,
and with bracelets on his wrists as a gift,
the supreme man shone with his morning attire.
By helping others, not by sandalwood paste— by generosity, virtue, renunciation, uprightness,
gentleness, austerity, freedom from anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition.
Ten kings should maintain these with heedfulness:
generosity, beneficial conduct, kind speech, and impartiality.
These four means of integration were proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.
Even kings do not obtain the fearlessness, security, and happiness that those who have died obtain from fire;
nor do they obtain it even through superior power when terrified.
But the wise, being afraid of the terror of saṃsāra, do not tremble.
Vigilance, rising from sleep, sharing, and seeking excellence—
these are the qualities of a leader that one who desires their own welfare should cultivate.
One who is mild is despised, while one who is excessively harsh incurs enmity.
Having understood both of these, one should practice with moderation.
It is not possible for one who is exclusively soft, nor for one who is exclusively harsh, to establish oneself in greatness; therefore, one should practice both.
The merchant Kassaka was his minister, and the ascetic Sutasoma was virtuous;
when these were born great, the kingdom too would be great.
When these were born weak, the kingdom too would be weak.
Therefore, one who bears the burden of a kingdom should protect that vast realm.
Just as one who plucks the unripe fruit from a large,
fruit-bearing tree may know its flavor but destroys its seed.
A king who rules his realm unrighteously is like a great fruit-bearing tree that knows the taste of its own fruit yet destroys the kingdom itself.
He is like one who plucks the ripe fruit from a great tree while it still bears more.
He discerns its flavor and does not forget its seed;
he who governs the kingdom according to Dhamma is like a great tree—
he discerns its flavor and does not lose the kingdom.
King Yocarāja ruled his kingdom unjustly;
that kṣatriya king became hostile toward all medicinal herbs.
Likewise, he was hostile toward the merchants who were engaged in the trade of goods.
A king who gives food and alms, who is not obstructed by his own pride,
who knows the excellent field for striking and is impartial in battle,
and who is victorious over those who are haughty— he prevails with his entire army.
In the same way, a kshatriya who practices unrighteousness while practicing violence against these two—
self-restraint and the life of celibacy— is struck down by his own arrogance. O great noble,
you have bent yourself crookedly by your own doing, not by that of another.
By a lord, by a king, by a provincial governor, or by a regional ruler;
by a son who has done evil to his mother,
or by a pupil who has done evil to his teacher.
King Nāgarehikatara and King Pāpapurohita:
among those performing merit and demerit,
they receive a sixth part and a single portion respectively.
A king should restrain everyone from evil;
therefore, while increasing merit alone, he should inspire confidence in the body of people.
The life of a fool is short, while that of a wise person is much longer.
Just as King Janaka was the sovereign of his people and the royal law was the sovereign over him, so it is with leadership:
those without a leader perish, as do those with too many leaders;
those with a sluggish leader perish, as do those with a very good leader.
Just as the tortoises, the fish, the hens, and the cows nourish their young, so did Rāhuṇa nourish his kinsmen.
Having entered the royal court, he did not receive honor from anyone else.
One who is neither a fool nor excessively dull-witted,
and who is never negligent, when he attains virtue, wisdom, and purity,
then he is not terrified by that [world], and he guards his secret.
Whether by day or by night, being wise in the affairs of state,
one who has been summoned should not hesitate, but should dwell in the king's service.
One should not wear clothing equal to that of the king, nor garlands, nor ointments.
A wise man should conduct himself like one of the king’s attendants, observing his gestures and demeanor.
The king should sport with his ministers, surrounded by his wives;
neither the ministers nor the king’s wives should reveal their true feelings.
Unagitated, not fickle, prudent, with senses restrained,
and endowed with the aspiration of the mind— one may dwell in the king’s residence.
One should not play with his wives, nor should one consort with them when gone into seclusion.
One should not take wealth through extortion, nor should one live under the king’s dominion.
One should not prize excessive sleep, nor drink intoxicating liquor;
one should not seek out the lair of wild beasts, nor should one live under the king’s dominion.
One who has been authorized should not mount a carriage-palanquin, a couch, a mat, a boat, or a chariot;
rather, he should live within the royal residence.
Being discerning, he should keep neither too far from nor too near to the king.
One should dwell face-to-face with mindfulness, eating only as much as one is truly content.
One becomes a friend to kings, yet one does not become a king through sexual intercourse;
for kings are quick to anger, like an eye struck by a thorn.
A wise and intelligent man, even when not being honored,
should speak harshly to a king who has entered his assembly. Having gained an opening,
he should seize that opening, but he must never flatter the king.
One should stand as if restrained by fire, yet dwell within the king's domain.
A kshatriya may even forcibly seize a son or a brother from villages, towns, kingdoms, or provinces.
One should remain silent and look on, not uttering even a single evil word.
Whether it be elephant-riders, charioteers, or foot-soldiers,
by attending to their work, the king increases their wages.
One should not go to the inner apartments of the king; one should dwell within the royal residence.
His bowstring would snap, his belly would swell, or even his bamboo staff would tremble;
it would turn against him—therefore, one should dwell within the royal residence.
One who is without a bow, one whose belly is like a fish,
one who is tongueless, one who is blind yet brave— such a person may dwell in the king’s residence.
One should not approach a woman excessively, seeing the exhaustion of one's vital energy.
One whose intellect is exhausted falls into a state of coughing, gasping, and rigidity.
One should not speak excessively, nor should one always remain silent;
one should utter measured speech that has not been overstepped, at the appropriate time.
Free from anger, not quarrelsome,
truthful, gentle, and free from slander;
one should not utter frivolous speech.
One should live in the king’s service if one is a supporter of mother and father, respectful toward the elders of the family,
and endowed with a sense of shame and moral dread. One should live in the king’s service.
One who has mastered the arts, who is self-restrained, disciplined, and gentle;
who is diligent, pure, and wise—such a person may dwell in the king’s service.
One who is humble in conduct toward elders, respectful and deferential, [should likewise live there].
Living in harmony with those who are gentle brings happiness;
one should dwell even in the presence of a king. One should avoid from afar people sent by the king to spy, and look only toward one’s own master, and not at other kings.
One should respectfully attend upon ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous and learned, gratifying them with food and drink.
Desiring one's own growth, one should approach them and ask questions.
One should not cause [others] to give what has already been given away to recluses and brahmins;
one should not obstruct anything at the time of giving to those who seek alms.
Possessing wisdom and endowed with growth, one is skilled in the methods of ritual procedure.
Knowing the right time and knowing the proper occasion, one should dwell in the king’s residence.
Rising early and diligent in one's duties, being heedful and circumspect,
with one's work well-organized, one should dwell in the king’s residence.
One who frequently goes to another's threshing floor, field,
or pasture should have only a limited amount of grain stored and should cook only a limited amount at home.
Even if one’s own son or brother is not established in virtuous conduct, [one should still exercise restraint].
The foolish women, driven by the god of love, were like those departed;
they trampled upon their cloths, their alms-food, and even the seats of others.
They were well-composed in virtue, yet they slept among slaves and laborers.
One who is endowed with the qualities of a wise counselor should be established in the position of sovereignty.
A king who possesses virtue and is free from greed,
who is compliant and devoted to his sovereign, should dwell openly within the royal residence.
May you live the life of a king, O King who knows the right time,
whose mind and speech are sovereign, and whose conduct is free from crookedness—
while being anointed, bathed, and having your feet washed and your head rubbed with fragrant oil.
One might even strike a lute, dwell in the service of a king, offer a pot with palms joined in reverence, or circumambulate a fire; yet what is the use of all these desires?
They do not provide the supreme, wise person with liberation.
Like the rain-cloud upon living beings, he showers them with wealth—
clothing for those who need it, vehicles, and houses for those who dwell in them.
These two, however, are like sharp thorns that pierce the body and wither one’s frame.
One who is destitute of sensual pleasures, one who is destitute of wealth, and one who is destitute of virtue—these are the three types of lowly characteristics: the destitute are ruined by hunger;
the weak are struck down by the strong; and the ignorant are defeated by the words and speech of others.
Three things on earth are sweet: sugar, a woman, and well-spoken words.
Sugar and women satisfy for a time, but well-spoken words satisfy forever.
Three jewels on the face of the earth are the means of gathering people together: sugar, a woman, and well-spoken words.
Skill, wealth, friends, and these four treasures— these four people, being deluded,
desire to go without them: one who seeks a good friend, one who wishes to cross a wilderness,
one who desires to speak in battle, and one who intends to travel on foot.
The five considered as "living" have been described in detail:
the suffering one, the sick one, the debtor, the one in debt, and the servant.
A person who possesses wisdom and is restrained regarding the sixfold group beginning with the eye-door—
There are seven types by virtue of moral conduct (*sīla*), and seven types by lack of moral conduct (*asīla*).

These are: one who is prone to sleep, one who is fond of intoxicants, one who is happy, one who is afflicted by disease, one who is young, one who lacks desire, and one who delights in work—these seven are excluded from the [remaining] teachers.
One who possesses noble lineage, wisdom, and eloquence, who maintains a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing,
is learned, desires the welfare [of others], and guards the [teachings]— these eight are yoked to the Teacher’s purpose.
Furthermore, one who is of excellent family, endowed with wisdom, brave in growth, and virtuous.
The learned, one who has renounced the world, the fearless, and one who goes to a happy destination—these nine are the best of people; they restrain themselves from evil.
The Buddha, the Paccekabuddha, the Arahant, and the chief disciple—these four are the supreme beings.
One should know that these five— the mother, the father, the teacher, the donor,
and the teacher of the Dhamma— are not to be betrayed by the wise.
They are the cause of the accomplishment of life for those who desire the Dhamma, the goal, sensual pleasure, and liberation.
What is destroyed when that [deceit] is destroyed?
Who is protected when that is protected? O All-Seeing One, deceit is the cause of long life for beings, while the absence of deceit is undoubtedly the cause of suffering for all.
Just as the ichor from the temples of an elephant in battle does not leave its source,
nor sandalwood its fragrance even when crushed, so too the wise man,
even when fallen into suffering, does not abandon the scent of his essential virtue.
Those who speak of happiness at a time when it is absent have abandoned the Dhamma.
To humans, the self is their kinsman; to living beings, the self is their enemy.
The self is one’s own relative; the self is one’s own enemy.
Only the virtuous protect those who depend on them by sacrificing even themselves;
they do not consider that to be a loss.
For the wise, time passes in the investigation of grammar and prosody.
Through the ruin of the wicked, or through sleep and quarreling, bees desire the flower; flies desire what is putrid;
the wise desire virtue, while the base desire faults.
Fruit-bearing trees bend, and wise people bend;
but dry wood and a fool do not bend—they break.
If they quarrel while still being whole, they will quickly join back together again.
The foolish covet even when they have fallen into calamity, yet they do not attain the state of the noble.
Even a small amount of wealth for the virtuous is a source of support like water in a well;
whereas even a vast amount for the wicked is not like water in the ocean.
Thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for fear come day after day to the deluded man, but not to the wise one.
For one with a corrupt mind and full of resentment, anger is engraved like a line upon stone.
For one who is base and of low birth, whose fame lasts but a short time,
who is gluttonous, discontented, ungrateful, and fickle—
it is impossible for such a person to ever train in noble conduct.
The earth possesses goodness through association with virtuous people who are free from wickedness,
and it possesses the lack of wickedness through association with the good who are free from wickedness;
likewise, the ground bears fragrance born of flowers.
They do not bear the fragrance of the earth nor the scent of flowers.
They smear their own virtues upon others and quarrel with them;
they proclaim even the slightest fault in one who reveals their own virtues.
They see the faults of others, but do not see their own fault;
they see a fault as small as a sesame seed, but do not see a fault as large as a coconut.
Anger does not know the true goal; anger does not perceive the Dhamma.
"That is a burning in blinding darkness" refers to the anger that seizes a person.
Anger born within certainly destroys one's wealth,
just as a fire in a beautiful basket filled with clothes and ornaments.
Lust is a thorn in the mind, a thief of the rope of virtues,
the eclipse of the moon of wisdom, and the fire that consumes the wealth of asceticism.
Even for the wise, there is no wealth equal to well-spoken words.
Even for one who is dissatisfied with the great waters of the ocean, which are lovely to behold, there is no loss;
yet even a lord of the earth is lost through lack of contentment.
Prostitution exists alongside those who are shameless, even among women of good family.
The king, the ocean, the singer, the artisan, the covetous person, and the fickle individual—among these who have great desires, such great desire is undesirable.
Health is the supreme gain; contentment is the supreme wealth.
The cessation of strife is supreme; Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.
O fool, go to a miserable state; gain is not filled by gain.
As rain upon dry land is not satisfied by water, so too gain is not filled by gain.
"O Bodhaya! Give! thus do people beg; "Give it to me," say the last-born folk.
"May there be no such thing as the fruit of giving"—thus [they think].
From a rock, a jewel; from an elephant, ichor; from a rutting elephant, musk.
Sandalwood is found here and there, and a wise man from place to place.
Among hundreds a hero is born, and among thousands a wise man;
among hundreds of thousands a speaker is found, but one who is truly generous is rare indeed.
One should praise a hero who has returned victorious, wealth that has come into the house,
food when one is old, and a wife who has reached her youth.
One should praise a craft even when it is found in books, and wealth even when it is in the hands of others.
When desire arises, there is neither craft nor wealth [to satisfy it].
Kings have speech as their weapon; ascetics have truth as their weapon;
merchants have wealth as their weapon; and the poor have oxen as their weapon.
They desire a hero in times of crisis, well-spoken words in times of tumult,
pleasant food and drink, and a wise man in matters of purpose.
One should support a friend in times of poverty, and store up grain in times of famine.
One who maintains a craft in the assembly, who brings about the gathering of wealth on this earth,
who gives food in times of famine and gold in times of plenty, who dispels fear in times of danger,
and who is both a restrainer and a non-restrainer toward all— [such a person is truly noble].
A crow does not shine in the midst of swans, nor does a tiger among sheep;
a donkey does not shine among horses, and a fool does not shine among the wise.
He who cannot conquer the unconquerable is no king, and he who cannot subdue his own self is no friend to himself.
One who knows not his parents does not honor them as husband and wife;
sons who do not oppose their elders are those by whom the aged are supported.
There is no friend equal to knowledge, and no enemy equal to disease.
There is no love equal to that for one's own self, and no power greater than that of karma.
There is no virtue in one who is lustful toward women,
and no purity in one who subsists on meat.
What is the drinking of liquor for those who are incapable? What is falsehood for those who are exceedingly wrathful?
Where is there too great a burden for those who are capable? How far is it for those who travel abroad?
For those who possess knowledge of the proper place and time,
for those who speak with gentleness and kindness: there is no famine for the wise,
no misfortune for the peaceful, no quarrel for the humble, and no fear for the vigilant.

The bee’s sting, the tip of the fly’s proboscis, the ascetics’ water-pot, the *setamba* fruit, and betel—these do not cause pain to one who is about to be born. The lute has five strings, the bow five joints, and the arrow five feathers. The bowman stands at seven cubits, and the fragrance of the lute extends for seven cubits. The arrow pierces for seven cubits, and the sound of the lute reaches for seven cubits. The lute is dear to the gods, and the bow is dear to the Asuras. The lute is dear to the Gandhabbas, and the bow is dear to the Dānavas. The lute is dear to the Gandhabbas, and the bow is dear to the Asuras. The impurity of a wife who is unfaithful for one month, and the impurity of a pupil who is unfaithful for half a month;
the impurity of a woman’s misconduct, the impurity of stinginess in one who gives,
the impurities of debt, of a fisherman, and of unrighteousness— these exist both in this world and in the world beyond.
Dirtier than dirt is ignorance—the supreme defilement.
Constant application to the protection of what has been heard is the clothing of a family; for a man, it is knowledge.
For a king who has brought about the subduing of his border regions, women are a protection for their husbands only so long as they have no other purpose.
But craving destroys the youth of living beings and destroys all happiness.
All power is destroyed by anxiety; compassion destroys one's own wealth.
Living in a lowly place destroys prosperity; being a beggar destroys what is honorable.
Praise destroys good qualities; lack of self-restraint destroys the mind.
For those who possess wealth, there is fear of its loss; for mortals, there is the fear of death;
but for all those who are supreme, the greatest fear is dishonor.
Even as the sun shines with its heat, it does not do so while surrounded by its retinue.
It has become cool with moonbeams, surrounded by stars;
here the analogy should be understood as that of the sun, the moon, and Rāhu.
The lazy one and the dull-witted one, the happy one and the one afflicted by disease.
It increases sleep and flesh, it is deluded by the craving for beauty;
negligence arises from intoxication, and from negligence arises decline.
From decline, faults increase; why, then, would a wise person not abandon intoxication?
As is the seed that is sown, such is the fruit one reaps:
the doer of good receives what is good, and the doer of evil receives what is evil.
He who speaks of the fruit of merit and demerit but does not believe it to be true—
One who does not believe in the welfare of the future life will quickly bring a mirror-surface to the forest of sleepers;
yet even such a person does not see the path leading to liberation for those who go to their dwelling places.
One who is endowed with these seven qualities— faith, moral shame, moral dread, great learning,
energy, mindfulness, and wisdom— is considered a wise person.
With faith as its root, virtue as its trunk, and wisdom as its leaves, it is a tree of heroism.
By treating the Buddha as a flower, the *garu* seed, and the *bharagu* fruit;
by treating books and the like as a field, writing as a pair of oxen and a plow,
and letters as seeds— one who acts in this way becomes wise.
If one should regard even a single syllable as equal to the form of the Buddha,
then a wise man indeed should write down the Three Pitakas.
The author of the Three Pitakas shall not be reborn in an evil state.
Many times he was a wheel-turning monarch, a sovereign lord of the four continents;
and countless times, beyond measure, he held extensive regional sovereignty.
Many times he became a king among the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens.
Performing meritorious deeds such as giving, one becomes a sprout of enlightenment;
endowed with all the factors of existence, one shall become honored by the three worlds.
When wealth and prosperity flourish, one is born into a most excellent family.
Association with the most excellent alone is [the way];
one who recites the Three Piṭakas, by the fruit of even a single syllable,
becomes a maker of the Three Piṭakas and attains eighty-four thousand noble forms of happiness.
Even with a small load, the wise and discerning person uplifts themselves,
like a traveler on a path carrying a burden. Suffering is the result of evil,
happiness that of merit, and mixed results come from mixed actions.
One goes with all that one has done; it should be known that there is no fruit apart from karma.
One who incites shares a fourth part, those who carry out the deed share three parts, the owner shares an equal part, and one who rejoices shares a single part.
Silence is supreme for one who speaks of non-self;
a single true friend is supreme among friends;
a beautiful wife is better than blindness.
The happiness of one who is far from evil is supreme.
Even if he is lowly, a man who exerts himself and possesses confidence,
being perfected in virtue and conduct, shines forth like a fire at night.
One does not become an outcast by birth,
nor does one become a brahmin by birth; it is by one's actions that one becomes an outcast, and by one's actions that one becomes a brahmin.
By action one becomes a brahmin.
The earth may tremble like a reed, the world-system may be as fragile as a fruit,
Mount Sineru may seem a mere molehill, and the ocean may appear as if it were tossed up by a foot.
In a single aeon, the mother’s milk [consumed] does not amount to a mere accumulation;
even more than that, it exceeds the waters of the great ocean.
Brahmā, the father, and the mother are called the original teachers.
They are worthy of offerings from their children and are compassionate toward all beings.
Therefore, a wise person should honor them and revere them with food, drink, clothing, and bedding.
By anointing him, by bathing him, and by washing his feet;
by rising for him and attending to his needs, the wise man should serve him.
They praise this very act here in this world, and he rejoices in the higher realms.
"In a single eon, the accumulation of bones of a single person would equal a mountain heap; thus it was said by the Great Seer.
Of all gifts, the gift of Dhamma is supreme."
One who has conquered the taste for all flavors through the Dhamma;
one who has conquered delight in all pleasures through the Dhamma;
one who has conquered all suffering through the destruction of craving.
Therefore, delight in heedfulness and guard your own mind;
pull yourself out from suffering, like an elephant from the mud.
Abandon association with the wicked and cultivate the company of the virtuous.
For one who has performed merit, the night is always like day.
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease. Their subsiding is blissful.
Both the Dhamma and the non-Dhamma have equal results:
the non-Dhamma leads to hell, while the Dhamma causes one to attain a happy destination.
